item.title: Navatu Secondary stun RKS 22-17 to create U19 Super Deans history
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 15/08/2026 Navatu Secondary School has created history as the first team from the North to reach the final of the Vodafone Fiji Secondary Schools Rugby Union Super Deans Competition after edging Ratu Kadavulevu School 22-17 in the U19 semi-final.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 15/08/2026

Navatu Secondary School has created history as the first team from the North to reach the final of the Vodafone Fiji Secondary Schools Rugby Union Super Deans Competition after edging Ratu Kadavulevu School 22-17 in the U19 semi-final.

Navatu Secondary came into the competition as underdogs and were the only team from the North competing in the Super Deans Competition.

They got off to a great start and kept the boys from Delanakaikai at bay in the first half.

RKS regrouped and came out strongly in the second half, closing the gap to 22-17 with a few minutes left to play.

Navatu’s defence was tested but held strong until the final whistle.

Navatu Secondary will now turn their focus to the final, where they will meet Lelean Memorial School, who defeated Ratu Navula College 36-27 at Churchill Park in Lautoka.

In other results, QVS defeated MGM High School 22-15, while Ratu Navula edged RKS 26-25 in the U14 semi-finals.

RKS came from behind to edge rivals Queen Victoria School 28-26, while Marist Brothers High School defeated Lelean Memorial School 16-3 in the U15 semi-finals.

QVS beat MGM High School 17-15, while Suva Grammar thrashed Nasinu Secondary School 22-0 in the U16 semi-finals.

RKS defeated Methodist High School 47-29, while Suva Grammar School overcame Queen Victoria School 32-24 in the U17 semi-finals.

item.title: FTUC targets 100,000 signatures in push for $8-an-hour living wage
item.description: The Fiji Trades Union Congress is targeting 100,000 signatures in three months in support of its campaign for an $8-an-hour National Living Wage in Fiji. FTUC Assistant National Secretary Jotika Sharma says the union movement is calling on the Government to establish a National Living Wage policy, which Fiji currently does not have.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Trades Union Congress is targeting 100,000 signatures in three months in support of its campaign for an $8-an-hour National Living Wage in Fiji.

FTUC Assistant National Secretary Jotika Sharma says the union movement is calling on the Government to establish a National Living Wage policy, which Fiji currently does not have.

Speaking to fijivillage News at Terry Walk in Suva today, Sharma says the campaign follows a decision made by FTUC delegates and members at the organisation’s annual conference in Nadi in May.

She says the proposed $8 hourly rate was determined based on the union’s surveys, data and views gathered from its members.

Sharma says FTUC has launched a three-month public campaign to gather signatures from workers and members of the public, with the aim of presenting the petition to the Government around the end of October to coincide with the World Day for Decent Work.

She says the campaign aims to address rising living costs and stagnant wages while establishing clear benchmarks for determining fair wages in Fiji.

Sharma says the campaign has been taken to the public to raise awareness of the need for a National Living Wage and build broad public support.

She adds that members of the public have already shown strong support at campaign stations in Suva, Nadi and Lautoka.

Sharma says the campaign also aims to address the issue of workers leaving Fiji in search of better wages overseas.

FTUC says members of the public who cannot visit the campaign stations can also support the initiative through its online platforms.

Sharma says the union is hopeful of reaching its target of 100,000 signatures before submitting its call to the Government.

item.title: Empower Pacific reports 20% rise in child suicide and self-harm referrals
item.description: A growing number of children and young people in Fiji are seeking help for suicidal thoughts, attempted suicide and self-harm, with Empower Pacific reporting a 20 percent increase in referrals involving children presenting with attempted suicide and self-harm in 2025. Speaking to fijivillage News, Empower Pacific Chief Executive Officer Patrick Morgam says the increase highlights the urgent need f
item.content:encoded:
A growing number of children and young people in Fiji are seeking help for suicidal thoughts, attempted suicide and self-harm, with Empower Pacific reporting a 20 percent increase in referrals involving children presenting with attempted suicide and self-harm in 2025.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Empower Pacific Chief Executive Officer Patrick Morgam says the increase highlights the urgent need for early intervention and stronger mental health support for young people across the country.

According to Morgam, data from the Fiji Police Force shows that 489 lives were lost to suicide between 2020 and 2024, while 446 attempted suicides were recorded during the same period.

I n 2024 alone, Fiji recorded 99 suicide deaths and 64 attempted suicides.

Young people remain particularly vulnerable, with data covering the first eight months of a recent reporting period showing 13 suicide deaths and 11 attempted suicides among those aged between 18 and 24.

Males account for about 70 percent of recorded suicide cases in Fiji, while the Western Division continues to record the highest proportion, accounting for approximately 43 percent of suicide cases and nearly half or more of recorded attempted suicides.

Morgam says Empower Pacific has also seen a significant number of children and young people seeking counselling and social support.

Between 2023 and late 2025, the organisation responded to 12,758 cases across its seven operational sites in Fiji, involving children, adolescents, young adults and families seeking assistance for a range of mental health and social issues.

He says the increase in referrals should be viewed not only as a concern but also as an indication that more young people and those around them are recognising the importance of seeking help.

He says these referrals come through hospitals, schools, communities, families and Empower Pacific’s 24/7 counselling helpline.

Morgam says Empower Pacific’s 24/7 helpline has also experienced increasing demand, with counsellors and social workers managing numerous calls during periods of heightened stress.

He says young people rarely seek help because of a single issue, with many experiencing a combination of emotional, social and environmental pressures.

These include depression, anxiety, stress, hopelessness and suicidal thoughts, as well as family conflict, domestic violence, neglect, substance abuse, bullying , cyberbullying and academic pressure.

He says trauma resulting from physical or sexual abuse, grief, loss and exposure to violence is also among the issues faced by young people seeking support.

Morgam says creating safe spaces where young people feel heard and supported is critical.

If you are facing issues and would like to speak to a counsellor, then you can call Empower Pacific toll free number 5626.

item.title: Fiji opens first adolescent drug recovery centre in Lautoka
item.description: Fiji’s first structured residential drug recovery programme specifically for teenage boys has opened in Lautoka, as concerns grow over alcohol and illicit drug use among children. Minister for Children, Sashi Kiran officially opened the Na Sala Vou Recovery Centre.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s first structured residential drug recovery programme specifically for teenage boys has opened in Lautoka, as concerns grow over alcohol and illicit drug use among children.

Minister for Children, Sashi Kiran officially opened the Na Sala Vou Recovery Centre.

The centre will provide a 12-week residential drug recovery programme for boys aged between 14 and 17.

Kiran says the opening is an important milestone in Fiji’s response to drug and alcohol use among young people, with children as young as 10 to 14 years being affected by addiction.

She says Fiji needs a coordinated and compassionate response that includes treatment, family support and greater community involvement.

Kiran says the focus should not only be on removing children from the streets, but also understanding why they end up there in the first place.

She is calling on families, communities, faith-based organisations and civil society groups to strengthen support for vulnerable children, saying traditional support systems, including the vanua, family and community, have an important role in protecting them from harmful influences.

Kiran further says children recovering from addiction also need continued support when they return to their families and communities after completing treatment.

She adds that the success of the Na Sala Vou Recovery Centre will depend not only on its three-month residential programme but also on the support children receive after leaving the centre.

Kiran also acknowledged Empower Pacific, the Punja’s Group of Companies, government agencies, faith-based organisations and civil society groups for supporting efforts to protect and rehabilitate children.

She described the centre as a new door to healing, hope and a new path for Fiji’s young people.

item.title: Heavy Rain Alert in force for parts of Fiji
item.description: Get ready for a wet weekend, with a Heavy Rain Alert now in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands. The Nadi Weather Office says a trough of low pressure is approaching from the west and will affect the western parts of the country until tomorrow.
item.content:encoded:
Get ready for a wet weekend, with a Heavy Rain Alert now in force for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands.

The Nadi Weather Office says a trough of low pressure is approaching from the west and will affect the western parts of the country until tomorrow.

Occasional rain, isolated heavy rainfall and thunderstorms are forecast for Viti Levu, Yasawa, Mamanuca, Kadavu and nearby smaller islands.

Other parts of the country can expect cloudy conditions.

item.title: ISS Fun Day celebrates diversity, culture and community
item.description: International School Suva is celebrating the diversity of its community as students, families and volunteers come together for the 2026 Fun Day. Head of School Jesse Donnelly says the event is about bringing the ISS community together and, most importantly, having fun.
item.content:encoded:
International School Suva is celebrating the diversity of its community as students, families and volunteers come together for the 2026 Fun Day.

Head of School Jesse Donnelly says the event is about bringing the ISS community together and, most importantly, having fun.

Donnelly says one of the exciting new additions to this year's Fun Day is the Fiji Arts Council community weaving project , which represents the diversity of the school and the 54 nationalities that make up the ISS community.

He says there is also a greater focus on sustainability this year, with cycling stations around the school and Green Team volunteers encouraging everyone to play their part in looking after the environment.

Donnelly also acknowledged the students who performed a traditional meke, saying it was a special way to welcome people to ISS and a reminder of the community and culture the school is fortunate to be part of in Fiji.

He thanked Timothy Ulacake and everyone involved in creating the new ISS Spirit Song, which was featured during the event.

Donnelly says he believes the Spirit Song is something the ISS community will hear many times in the years ahead.

He also acknowledged the school's PTA and the many volunteers who have spent countless hours over the past few months preparing for Fun Day.

Donnelly thanked them for their energy, generosity and commitment, saying the event would not have been possible without their support.

Th Head of School encourages students, families and visitors to enjoy the food and activities, spend time together and, most importantly, have fun, with the event set to close at 2pm.
